summary: Lists the requirements that a middlebox communication (midcom) protocol must satisfy so applications can influence middlebox behavior. The focus is on network address translators and firewalls. It states needs rather than defining the protocol itself.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3304 lists what a Middlebox Communication (midcom) protocol must do when an application asks a firewall or network address translator to change its behavior. It sets requirements for clear results, predictable rules, and secure communication, but does not define the protocol itself.

subtitle: Requirements for a protocol that lets applications request services from firewalls and NATs.

tldr.problem: Applications may need to request actions from middleboxes such as firewalls and network address translators, so a communication protocol needs clear requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for authorized communication, predictable behavior, rule management, filtering, error reporting, and security.
tldr.outcome: It states requirements rather than defining a protocol. RFC 3303 provides the framework and terminology the document uses.

today: RFC 3304 is an Informational RFC published in August 2002. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document describes requirements rather than a protocol.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
This document gives requirements for a protocol between a middlebox and a midcom agent, an entity that asks the middlebox for a service. The focus is on firewalls and network address translators.

The requirements were drawn from the midcom framework in RFC 3303, which supplies related context and terminology and is intended to be read with this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A midcom agent sends requests to a middlebox, such as a firewall. This RFC lists requirements for the communication between them.

sections.title: Communication and Session Requirements
sections.content:
The protocol must let an agent establish an authorized association with a middlebox, and both sides must authenticate each other. An agent may communicate with several middleboxes, and a middlebox may serve several agents; when their requests interact, the result must be deterministic.

The parties must be able to reach a known state, including after a failure, and release resources used by a failed element. A middlebox must report its status and may send an unsolicited message about an event such as closing a pinhole. Either party may end a session, and an agent must learn whether a request succeeded.
sections.plainLanguage: The agent and middlebox must know who they are communicating with and whether each request worked. The protocol must also handle failures and competing requests in a predictable way.

sections.title: Rules, Options, and Error Reporting
sections.content:
The protocol syntax and meaning must allow extensions. An agent must be able to install rules for more than one middlebox action, group rules so one message can manage them together, and extend a ruleset's lifetime. Multiple authorized agents must be able to work on the same ruleset.

When a peer does not understand an option, the protocol must make clear whether it can continue without the option or must reject the request. Failure reasons must help an agent adapt without making attacks easier. Filters must be able to include a five-part description: source address and port, destination address and port, and transport protocol.

For port mapping, the protocol should support requests that preserve whether a port is odd or even and map consecutive external ports to consecutive internal ports. A more specific filter should be able to override an overlapping ruleset.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol must let agents manage groups of rules and describe which traffic a rule covers. If an option or request fails, the response must explain enough for the agent to react without exposing the system to attack.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The protocol must provide message authentication, confidentiality, and integrity. Confidentiality for control messages must be optional; when provided, the mechanism should allow a choice of algorithm.

The protocol must work securely across untrusted domains and define ways to reduce replay attacks against control messages. The RFC's Security Considerations section refers to these requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages must be checked for sender identity and tampering. The protocol must also protect control messages from being copied and replayed later.

sections.title: Requirements, Not a Protocol Design
sections.content:
RFC 3304 is a list of requirements for designers of a midcom protocol. It covers how agents and middleboxes communicate, how they manage rules, and how the protocol protects their messages.

The document does not specify message formats or an implementation. Its framework companion is RFC 3303.
sections.plainLanguage: This document gives protocol designers a checklist, not a finished protocol. RFC 3303 provides the related framework.
